extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of art history; practicing painters and patrons interested in Renaissance Florentine painting
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative language for judging or producing Renaissance (Florentine) panel and fresco paintings — technical, compositional, and moral qualities illustrated by the lives and works of Fra Bartolommeo and Mariotto Albertinelli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proficiency in colouring and drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Success and reputation derive from excellence both in colouring and in drawing (e.g., 'he acquired the name and reputation of being one of the best young men of his art, both in colouring and in drawing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: early Madonnas and panel works praised for colouring and draughtsmanship; companionship and imitation between masters can transmit manner. Proficiency is shown across genres (panel, fresco) and noted by patrons and collectors who prize such works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and beauty of manner (especially in fresco)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should be executed with diligence and a pleasing manner ('executed with such diligence and beauty of manner... that he acquired extraordinary fame').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finished portions should show careful execution and an attractive manner; even unfinished works may reveal the quality of the executed parts. Diligence contributes to professional reputation and patronal commissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive depiction of emotion and narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures must communicate appropriate emotions and narrative states (e.g., in the Judgment fresco 'one sees the despair, grief, and shame of everlasting death' and 'contentment and gladness in those that are being saved').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ gestures, facial expression, and body posture to convey story and moral affect; such expressiveness is praised as a mark of mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miniature-like precision for small-scale scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Small figures and door panels should be executed with the delicacy and precision of miniatures ('little figures after the manner of miniatures... not possible to do better work in oils').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working on small doors, tabernacles, or minute scenes, aim for miniature-level detail and finish; such works can be treasured by patrons and collectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and blending of colour to produce relief and life
rubrics_metrics.description: Blending of colouring should create harmony and make figures appear in relief and alive ('introduced a method of blending the colouring of his figures... making them appear to be in relief and alive').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour transitions and tonal blending are central to making painted figures read as living bodies and to unify multi-figure compositions; imitation of masters (e.g., Leonardo) may inform this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and management of dark tones (influence of Leonardo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of darks and blacks (e.g., use of printer's smoke-black and black of burnt ivory) to model forms and shadows, following Leonardo's example ('he imitated to a great extent the works of Leonardo; particularly in the darks...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dark pigments can give strong relief but carry conservation risks: heavy blacks may darken over time and change the appearance of the work; choose and apply blacks with awareness of long-term effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good drawing, gesture, and vivacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures should be drawn with lifelike gesture and vivacity so they appear active and believable (e.g., children playing instruments drawn so lifelike 'whoever beholds him cannot persuade himself that he should not also hear the voice').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to small actions, physical posture, and the relationship between figure and instrument or prop enhances verisimilitude and expressive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chiaroscuro and fine gradation of shadows for force and relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Use chiaroscuro and careful gradation of shadow to give force and make figures stand out from the picture ('strong relief by a fine gradation of dark shadows').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between light and dark is used deliberately to model volume and to create the illusion of relief; too little or too harsh shadow can harm clarity or subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate perspective and spatial distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Design figures and architectural settings with convincing perspective and distribution so groups recede naturally ('a circle of saints... diminishing in perspective... distributed with such fine design that they seem to be real').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use perspective to order large compositions and to distribute figures across planes; receding tones and architectural cues strengthen depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical truth and convincing treatment of nudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to paint nudes convincingly in form and flesh-colour ('painted a picture of S. Sebastian, naked, very lifelike in the colouring of the flesh...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying the nude and demonstrating lifelike flesh-colour and anatomy is a high standard; success may provoke strong public reaction (positive or scandalous) depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative presentation and framing solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovate in presentation (e.g., painting a frame into the panel or shaping the panel to avoid physical frames) to solve practical/display issues ('he caused the panel to be made in the form of a half-circle... painting a frame all round').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design decisions about panel shape, painted architectural frames, or trompe-l'oeil niches can prevent frames from obscuring figures and can enhance the work's integration with its setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory work: cartoons and drawings before colouring
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch and prepare cartoons or ink/bitumen drawings before applying colour ('sketching them in the manner of a cartoon, with ink or with bitumen, before colouring them...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cartoons and preparatory drawings to resolve design, composition, and figure placement; preserved beginnings and drawings attest to workshop practice and intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study from life and use of movable models
rubrics_metrics.description: Work from living models and practical devices (e.g., articulated wooden model clothed in real draperies) to observe drapery, posture, and detail ('he caused a life-size figure of wood to be made, which moved at the joints; and this he clothed with real draperies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping live references or mechanical models aids consistency in drapery, foreshortening, and repeated figure types; such devices are practical studio technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between delicacy and force in tonal treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine delicacy of colour/finish with sufficient shadow-force so figures have both refinement and relief ('wished to combine this delicacy with a certain method of treatment... pictures which have no relief and force, combined with delicacy, are of no account').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremes: shadows too dark make forms indistinct; too delicate and they lack force. Seek a method that yields both refinement and three-dimensional presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: High finish and draughtsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical finish and precise draughtsmanship are markers of quality ('executed with excellent draughtsmanship and high finish').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to fine finish on faces, hands, draperies and important details; patrons and craftsmen value high finish as a sign of mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional skill in multi-figure and crowded scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to arrange a large number of figures coherently and gracefully ('a panel with an infinite number of figures... many figures surrounding a Madonna, all most admirable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition must preserve clarity and hierarchy even in crowded scenes: use grouping, perspective, and tonal control to maintain legibility and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material choice and technical longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pigments and techniques that stand the test of time and avoid practices that cause cracking or spoilage ('it is all cracking and spoiling, on account of its having been painted with fresh coats of colour on fresh size').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of substrate and layering methods: applying fresh paint over unseasoned ground or incompatible media can cause conservation issues; technical knowledge of materials is part of quality execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveying spiritual or 'celestial' quality in sacred subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Paintings of sacred subjects should convey a spiritual radiance or celestial quality perceptible to the attentive viewer ('there is clearly perceived in him a certain celestial quality... which seems... to shine out over that work').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical skill, aim to communicate devotional intensity and spiritual presence through composition, expression, and colour harmony; this intangible quality greatly enhances religious works' value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of subject to moral and institutional context
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose subject matter appropriate to patrons' religious and moral expectations (e.g., removal of works judged lascivious; burning of nude studies in civic-religious purges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience and setting (convent, public square, chapel): what is acceptable in one context may be censured in another. Moral suitability can affect a work's display and survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color experimentation and pursuit of specific optical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with pigments and whites to achieve desired brilliance or effects (e.g., attempting to make lead-white more brilliant), as part of striving for ideal visual outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical experimentation can yield novel effects but must be balanced against material stability; striving for higher chromatic values (brighter whites, clearer tones) is part of an artist's pursuit but carries risk.
